At a minimum, the lesson here is that UML is just fucking garbage. -- Brian Will

Object-oriented programming is only a disaster because people took it too far in languages like Java in forcing everything to be an object.

A nice blend of OO, Functional, and Procedural code is optimal, in my opinion.
Java had primitives. Ruby is all objects.

Rolls eyes... There is no right way for everything. Every different solution to a problem comes with its own pluses and minuses. Weighing those against alternate solutions will point you to the right way to handle the task at hand. OOP is great for some things, functional for some things and procedural for smaller applications perhaps.

Procedural code is not typically reusable though. But if you have a small, one off task, it will be the fastest to get done. Those small one off things have a nasty habit of becoming bigger beasts though. YAGNI still applies I suppose.

The first example, processing a csv file and putting the data into a database, isn't really complicated enough for the structure to really matter. The only critical issue with that example is abstracting out file paths and user credentials. Otherwise the task for this example is a straightforward procedure.

The second example is such a clunky programming exercise I would assume it was originally chosen for its didactic value, since there is nothing practical about a coin flipping program.

In the third example, Will takes actual structured code and turns it into a maintenance nightmare. I have seen this type of thinking in a production system, "Hey, let's just turn these nested conditionals into a switch statement with 25 cases." Depending on the lifespan of the project, it can become a complete quagmire. It also tends to propagate itself into other code, since the choice of conditional logic (instead of a collection of objects) here will mean there is no layer of abstraction for other code to take advantage of, and another process, possibly dealing with the exact same collection of meaningless strings, will have to use switch logic as well. Using procedural code here is a decision to choose the option with loads of technical debt.

In the fourth example, Will shows that his procedural approach is better by producing an object oriented design. I am confused how this supports his original thesis that OO code is bad.

I have to agree with you on the first two examples, they were both so simple that they could only be used as exercises in object-orient programming.

In the third case I can see an argument for keeping an object-oriented approach - the solution that he took and turned into a procedural approach was very minimal and easy to understand even as an object-oriented solution because the main class and all the subclasses used were right there in the encapsulating class, and all the subclasses were simply implementing a single method. Turning it into a procedural method with the switch statement really just reduced the amount of code, without increasing the readability or maintainability any.

I would actually argue that using functional programming would be a better solution for the third case, because that's very nearly what the original solution was doing already.

I think in the 4th example, Will was trying to demonstrate that you can create more procedural code inside of an object-oriented design instead of going to the extremes that the original example went to. The fact that he didn't make the entire thing procedural was because then it would actually be a mess of spaghetti code and very difficult to read. He did, however, reduce the number of classes and the number of methods and fields within each object by writing each of the objects in a more procedural way.

Now that I look more closely, the third example is really only using objects as a datatype (the objects only have methods and have no properties) which would seem to indicate it is a functional approach, so not really a good example of OO in the first place.

Well, (looking at the third example again) it's really functional programming wrapped in the guise of OOP - were I writing that solution in JavaScript, I would simply have a map of { string: function() } relationships and pull from the map as necessary, but the example in the video chose to wrap a single method within a class and call that particular method on each of the classes as necessary, which I suppose is the next best thing to pure function references.

Thank you. As someone who just started coding is there a place you would recommend starting?

99% of people would recommend some language, usually something that has a large open source community surrounding it. I think that provides way too much of a safety net, if you are stumped by a problem and it only takes you 5 minutes to find a solution on Google then you are going to solve your problem but not benefit from the experience of trying lots of wrong things. Also everyone wants something practical they can use later on, but that just makes them more likely to get stuck in a rut, they get attached to the first tool they use, they cling to its idiosyncrasies and never know what else is out there.

So my recommendation is to go to Google Drive and create a new Google Sheets document. The spreadsheet is your canvas. You will need to create a challenge for yourself to make the spreadsheet do something interesting, but here's one to start: write a program that whenever you put an 'x' in one of the cells, your program will draw a dot '.' in the surrounding cells. The first thing you will have to figure out is how to attach code to the spreadsheet. They use a language call Apps Script that is based on Javascript. You will have to learn a bunch of useless things about Apps Script to get your code working, and you will never have a use for that knowledge outside of the Google platform, but you will pick up some skills in the process - or perhaps you will fail miserably. Good luck.

  3. Using a thermoelectric module to convert waste heat from the exhaust into electricity. A few manufacturers have looked into the technology, but it doesn't seem as though it will ever be viable.

I was pretty young when I came up with all of these ideas (16-17), so I couldn't have done anything to develop them, I don't know why I was so angry when I saw that people had already come up with them.

I'm fairly certain that I came up with the idea of a digital music player that used solid state media long before I had ever seen an MP3 player. I have a drawing of one that is either from the late '90s, or just after the year 2000. I had even come up with my own form of flash memory that somewhat resembled a small floppy disk. I had probably seen some kind of solid-state memory card (probably a compact flash card, or an early SD card) that stored a considerable amount of data and thought that it would be great for storing data from audio CDs. The last civil war was carried out with what were relatively crude weapons. Imagine the previous civil war fought modern weaponry. Replace a handloaded artillery bombardment with one destroyer or bomber with guided weapons. You would have a scenario were each side could actively target and engage all targets with relative ease. It would basically be two factions continuously pummel each other with relatively precise strikes to all targets of value. You would have to groups utilizing there offensive capabilities in a way to maximize the use of their offensive before their offensive capabilities is stopped by their opponents offensive capabilities.Logistically it would be a exercise in the ridiculous. You would have to feed any force your fielding and any force capable of a significant a significant action would be targeted by precision strike and any resource capable of feeding the significant for could also be be easily targeted. In effect you wouldn't be able to field a large force and would need to resort to what would be a largely urban guerilla force which would need to behave in the fashion of insurgents in contested regions of the Middle East. You would shed most of your technology to avoid aerial strike and carry out small scale skirmishes to harry the opposing forces. It strikes me that groups of people actively engaging one another while attempting to disrupt supply lines and the industry which provides the supplies would have at least some negative impact on the economy and the overall quality of life. So industry would seem to have the choice of supplying neither side or risk destruction by supporting one side. I suppose they could supply both sides in attempt to, for lack of a better word, profit but given the increasingly diminishing returns as any conflict continued and the likely disruption of normal commerce would seem to shutdown industry anyway. So the few locally manufactured goods are out, technology is risky use if used at all as I would think aerial bombardment and guerilla strikes would have at least some negative impact on the power grid which is not nearly as profitable maintain, roadways are disrupted as they are destroyed and are no longer profitable to maintain, education is disrupted as students are called to fight or kept out of harms way, and food supplies are logistical quandaries. Basically most things important to modern life are removed and access to necessities such as food and water are limited as they are needed for the war effort and impacted by the war itself. Commerce is crippled as industry is destroyed either physically or as a result of the decay of the infrastructure and key shipping ports are eliminated by the same action. Civilization would grind itself apart. This is of course under the assumption that opposing forces are equally matched and actively pursuing victory by destroying their opponents. If forces are asymmetrical and there is more of a revolutionary war type situation we would have the smaller group committing what is perceived as treason. They would be labeled as terrorists and actively pursued using all technological means and force into insurgency. Being unable to field any significant force at risk of having said for hit with a precision strike they would be forced to resort to guerilla tactics which would be referred to as terrorism. With diminishing supplies and continued pressure by the opposition they would be forced into small off grid groups who risked being reported by the unsympathetic population and met with a superior force or precision strike whenever they took any significant action. If both sides focused on preserving infrastructure and life we would have quite a bit of posturing but limited action as each side would avoid direct action in order to preserve infrastructure resulting in a long but largely unproductive conflict which could be argued to be quite similar to the current state of affairs. People seem focused on a civil war or revolution being quite similar to the previous civil war or revolution and I really don't think they would have any similarity or positive outcome. We would either maintain status quo, become a militant Amish society or grind our civilization into a war-torn third world country. I think my solitary nature and survival skills would allow me to survive but at a level which would be considerably less comfortable than what I currently experience. I would suggest weighing any benefits against potential costs of any armed conflict before engaging in any such conflict. A good way to simulate the experience would be to turn off any devices which are connected to the internet, eat only the food you hunt or grow yourself, generate your own power, provide your own medical care, and watch for a precision strike any time you act in an observable manner.
